Before the tasks

One example, followed through every task

Abstract statements are easier to follow with something concrete in hand. Every section below shows what happens to the same three real tokens. They always appear in a dashed box like these.

Token A · id 2420 " एक"

Hindi for "one", with the space in front. It comes from the sentence भारत एक देश है ("India is a country"), which the tokenizer splits as 66526 · 2420 · 13092 · 732.

7 bytes: 20 e0 a4 8f e0 a4 95, a space and two complete letters. An ordinary token.

Token B · id 39329 ஸ் (its tail)

From the Tamil word மிஸ் ("miss"), split as 4475 · 19844 · 39329. The letter ஸ is 3 bytes, e0 ae b8, and the split falls inside it.

4 bytes: b8 e0 af 8d, the last byte of ஸ and then the sign ் (pulli). A piece of a character.

Token C · id 74642 ம் (its tail)

From ம்ம் ("hmm"), split as 4475 · 15336 · 74642. The letter ம is e0 ae ae, and again the split falls inside it.

4 bytes: ae e0 af 8d, the last byte of ம and then ். Also a piece.

B and C differ only in their first byte, and neither first byte is a character on its own. Ask the tokenizer to print them and both come out as �். That single fact drives most of Week 1.

Task 1 · Tables

Turn every token into bytes, two ways

The lab askedBuild the decode table and the raw byte table for P=32 and P=64. Put the code in teams/04-ke2/src/build_tables.py. The raw byte table must fix this.

In plain words

A table has one row per token: the bytes the encoder will read for it. The decode table does what the repository does today: print the token, then take the bytes of the printout. The raw byte table reads the token's true bytes straight from the tokenizer file. Each row has at most P byte slots.

Why it matters

The decode table reproduces the known issue so we can measure it. The raw table is the fix. Building both, at both sizes, shows exactly what the fix changes and whether more slots help.

How we did it

  1. Load the tokenizer, and refuse any file whose SHA-256 is not the pinned one (ke2.tokenizer).
  2. Decode table: print every token with decode([id]), the repository's current path, and cut long rows without splitting a character.
  3. Raw table: turn every token's piece back into bytes with the byte map, and cut long rows at P bytes. No token is long enough to be cut.
  4. Pack each table in the repository's layout and save it as compressed .npz, with a content hash bound to the tokenizer (ke2.tables).
  5. Test that the decode table equals upstream's build_byte_buffer and that the raw table fixes the known issue (tests/test_tables.py).

Why two tables: the known issue

Some tokens hold only part of a character. The tokenizer does this for rare characters, such as those of Santali (Ol Chiki script) or Manipuri (Meetei Mayek). Ask it to print one such piece on its own and it cannot, because half a character is not a character, so it prints �. The repository builds each token's row from that printout. So hundreds of different pieces all become the same row, and the same code.

The idea

Printing is a many-to-one step: different broken byte strings print as the same mark. Anything computed from the printout inherits that loss. The fix is to compute from what the tokenizer stores, not from what it prints.

The maths

Let λ(y) mean: read y as UTF-8, replace each broken sequence with U+FFFD, and turn the result back into bytes. The repository's row is fdec(t) = λ(fraw(t)). λ changes nothing on valid UTF-8, but it is not injective on broken input: λ(e1) = λ(ff) = ef bf bd. So fdec is not injective: 1,151 tokens fall into 10 sets with equal rows. fraw is injective on this vocabulary (all 131,072 differ), and Theorem 1 carries that over to the codes.

The lab named this the known issue and asked for a raw byte table that fixes it. This task builds both tables. Task 2 measures the issue and the fix. Task 3 proves that once the rows are different, the codes are different too.

Worked example · Task 1 at P = 32
TokenRaw byte table rowDecode table rowWhy

20 e0 a4 8f e0 a4 95

Reading B's raw row. The tokenizer file stores B as the piece ¸à¯į, one stand-in character per byte. The byte map undoes the swap: ¸ → b8, à → e0, ¯ → af, į → 8d. The first three are printable and stand for themselves; į is the stand-in for 8d, one of the 68 bytes that get a substitute (concept 3).

Storing it. Each row gets P = 32 byte slots plus a length. B fills 4 slots and the length is 4. At P = 64 the same bytes go in, with 32 more empty slots. No token comes close to 32 bytes, so nothing is ever cut.

The point. In the raw byte table B and C keep different rows. In the decode table they end up with the same row, so they would get the same code.

Result

Both decode tables match the repository exactly. 1,306 tokens print differently from their true bytes. The longest token is exactly 32 bytes, so no row is ever cut, at P = 32 or P = 64.

The idea

Both tables answer one question: which bytes does this token stand for? The decode table reads the printout, like a photocopy that blurs torn letters. The raw table reads the stored piece, the original page. Building both, at both sizes, measures exactly what the printout loses and whether more slots would help.

The maths
  • fraw(t) = β−1(piece(t)) (concept 3); special tokens use their literal text.
  • fdec(t) = the bytes of decode([id]). For every id it equals λ(fraw(t)): the raw bytes with broken parts replaced by U+FFFD (proof.md, section 4).
  • Cut rules: the decode table steps back over continuation bytes, as upstream's utf8_safe_truncate does; the raw table cuts plain bytes. Neither cuts anything here: the longest token has 32 bytes.
  • Row stored as B ∈ {0…255}V×P and lengths ℓ ∈ {0…P}V, with B[t, p] the row's byte for p < ℓt and 0 otherwise.
  • Measured (results/tables/manifest.json): 129,931 unique decode rows against 131,072 raw; 1,326 decode rows contain U+FFFD against 20 raw rows, the tokens that really hold that character.

  • Code: src/build_tables.py with the shared src/ke2/ package (tokenizer, truncation, tables). Tables by Swati (#7), compressed in #99.
  • Files: results/tables/{decode,raw}_table_P{32,64}.npz, about 0.8 MB each, and results/tables/manifest.json with their content hashes.

Task 2 · Collisions

Find every shared code and say why

The lab askedCount collisions per script class. Write teams/04-ke2/results/collisions.csv with a cause for each group.

In plain words

We find every group of tokens whose rows are identical, show why they match, and count them per writing system (Devanagari, Tamil, Latin and so on).

Why it matters

The Saturday check requires that each token has a unique code or a collision with a known cause. A cause only counts as known if we can show how it happens. Counting per script shows which languages are affected.

How we did it

  1. Group token ids with identical rows (src/collisions/build_collisions.py). By Theorem 1 these are exactly the ids with identical codes.
  2. Name each group's cause: empty, duplicate_vocab, special_literal, decode_collapse (true bytes differ, but the printout made them equal through �) or truncation. Anything else is other, and a test requires zero of it.
  3. Give every token a script class from its true bytes (ke2.script_class). A piece of a character is labelled Partial-UTF8[…], with the script or block its lead bytes point to.
  4. Write collisions.csv (one row per group, every member id), collisions_summary.csv (per table and script class) and collisions_meta.json (totals).
  5. Test it: every group is a real collision, the groups cover exactly the non-unique rows, and the committed CSV is current (tests/test_collisions.py).
Worked example · Task 2 on tokens B and C
  1. Sort into buckets by row. In the decode table B and C both have the row ef bf bd e0 af 8d. No other token has it, so this bucket holds exactly these two: group_id 4 of the decode table.
  2. Rule out causes. Their rows are only 6 bytes long, so no cut was involved, and their true bytes differ (b8 … and ae …), so they are not duplicates.
  3. Name the cause. Read b8 e0 af 8d as UTF-8. b8 is a continuation byte with no start byte in front, so it is broken and prints as �. e0 af 8d is the complete sign ். The same happens to ae e0 af 8d. True bytes differ, printouts agree: decode_collapse (in proof.md, bad_bytes_in).
  4. Count per script. The only complete character in each token is ், a Tamil sign, so both are classed Partial-UTF8[Tamil], and this group adds 2 colliding tokens to that class.

Raw byte table: B and C keep different rows, so they are in no group. Token A is in no group in either table.

Their row in results/collisions.csv: decode, 32, 4, decode_collapse, Partial-UTF8[Tamil], …, 2, 39329;74642, efbfbde0af8d, 6.

Result

Decode table: 10 groups, all caused by �. 1,151 tokens share them, so 1,141 codes are lost. Raw table: no groups at all, at P = 32 and P = 64. Every token has a unique code.

The same 10 groups at P = 32 and P = 64: 1,151 tokens, 1,141 codes lost, every one decode_collapse. Every member id is in results/collisions.csv, and Playground 2 opens each group.

The idea

Sort the tokens into buckets by their row. A bucket holding two or more tokens is a collision group. For each bucket, ask why its tokens look alike, and accept the answer only if a check reproduces the mechanism on every member.

The maths
  • s ~ t ⇔ TP(s) = TP(t) is an equivalence relation. Its classes split the vocabulary into buckets.
  • Collision groups are the classes with |G| ≥ 2. By Theorem 1 they are exactly the sets of tokens with equal codes.
  • Codes lost = V − (number of classes) = ΣG (|G| − 1). Decode table: 1,151 − 10 = 1,141 = 131,072 − 129,931.
  • decode_collapse for a group with shared row r: the members' true bytes differ, but their printouts all equal r, and r contains ef bf bd. truncation: the full strings differ but agree on the bytes that are kept.
  • Script class c(t) comes from fraw(t). Per class c: tokens and colliding tokens (collisions_summary.csv).

Task 3 · Proof

Prove the code never merges two different strings

The lab askedWrite Lemma 1, Lemma 2 and Theorem 1 in teams/04-ke2/proof.md, with numerical checks.

In plain words

The proof shows that the codec can never give two different byte strings the same code, and that a string can always be read back from its code. It is proof.md (Subramanya, #75), and its tests check every claim with numbers. This section explains it step by step, with the figures of proof_explained.md.

Why it matters

Counting shared rows (Task 2) tells us about codes only if the codec itself never merges two strings. The proof closes that gap: two codes are equal exactly when the cut strings are equal.

The three results, plainly

  • Lemma 1. The codec is injective. Each byte lights one cell in its own position, normalizing leaves two values far apart, and the lit cells give the string back.
  • Lemma 2. The repository's cut rule keeps a valid start of at most P bytes, never splits a letter, and can empty only a broken long token.
  • Theorem 1. Two tokens get the same code exactly when they are fed the same cut string, and a shared code has one of five causes.

The logic in two steps

Lemma 1, step 1

Each byte lights one cell in its own position, so the lit cells spell out the string.

+
Lemma 1, steps 2 and 3

Normalizing leaves two values: lit cells above 15.9, every other cell between −0.063 and 0.

=
So (steps 4 and 5)

The string can be read back from its code: the codec is injective.

Lemma 1

The codec is injective on strings of at most P bytes.

+
Lemma 2

The cut rule makes every fed string fit in P bytes.

=
Theorem 1

Same code exactly when same cut string. A shared code has one of five causes.

Why a proof is needed at all

The collision count compares table rows. It says something about codes only if the codec never merges two different rows on its own. In principle it could, in three places:

  1. Two bytes could light the same cell, and the codec adds up whatever lands together. Lemma 1, step 1 rules this out.
  2. Normalizing uses a shift and a stretch that depend on the string itself, so two different strings could end up as the same numbers. Lemma 1, steps 2 to 5 rule this out.
  3. Rounding in float32, or in bf16 and fp16 during training, could blur the values. proof.md's remark on floating point, and proof_explained.md for fp16, rule this out.

The cut rule can merge strings, by cutting two long tokens to the same start. Lemma 2 and the corollary of Theorem 1 say exactly when.

Result

All three are proven in proof.md. tests/test_lemma1.py, test_lemma2.py and test_theorem1.py check them on synthetic strings in fp32 and bf16, and test_proof_checks.py on all 131,072 tokens of the real tokenizer (results/proof_checks.json). proof_explained.md adds the figures, worked examples, bounds for every string length, the room for error, and fp16.

How to read Task 3

  1. Start with the guided playground just below: the whole argument on tokens A, B and C, in eight steps.
  2. Build a code by hand from your own text in Playground 3.
  3. Learn the symbols, the encoder and Lemma 2, and try the cut-rule playground.
  4. Work through Lemma 1 in two parts, the lit cells (Playground 3a) and normalizing (3b), then Theorem 1 (3c).
  5. Finish with the numerical checks.

The encoder, line by line

This is the code the proof is about, from codec.py in the kronecker-embeddings repository (commit d07cb54), unchanged. The comment on each line names what it computes.

lin_idx = bytes_long * pos_dim + pos                            # line 85   cell of byte v at position p: v·P + p
valid = pos < lens_long.unsqueeze(1)                            # line 88   only positions p < L count
scales = torch.rsqrt(lens_long.clamp_min(1).to(torch.float32))  # line 92   each lit cell is 1/√L
src = valid.to(torch.float32) * scales.unsqueeze(1)             # line 93
out = torch.zeros((B, D), device=device, dtype=torch.float32)   # line 98   D = 256·P zeros
out.scatter_add_(dim=1, index=lin_idx, src=src)                 # line 99   light the cells
mean = out.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)                           # line 102  m
std = (out - mean).std(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + eps              # line 103  σ = √v + ε (unbiased, divides by D − 1)
out = (out - mean) / std                                        # line 104  z(x) = (x − m) / σ
  • scatter_add_ adds. If two lit cells coincided they would add up. Lemma 1, step 1 shows they never do, so every lit cell is exactly 1/√L.
  • Line 70 rejects input that is not exactly P positions wide, and padding positions p ≥ L get weight 0 (line 88). Only the first L ≤ P bytes are encoded, which is why strings must fit (Lemma 2 (b), (c)).
  • std divides by D − 1, PyTorch's default. Lemma 1, step 2 uses exactly this.

Lemma 2: the cut rule and its six properties

In plain words

The encoder has room for P bytes per token. A longer token is cut: the repository keeps the longest start of at most P bytes that does not split a character, trying P, P − 1, P − 2 and P − 3 bytes. If none of those four is valid text, it keeps nothing.

The idea

Cutting is the one step before the codec that can make two tokens look alike. To account for every collision we need to know exactly what it can and cannot do. It never changes a short token, never splits a character, and never empties valid text. It can only empty a long token that is broken right from the start.

The statement in proof.md, section 2, for every byte string r and P ≥ 4
  1. (a) · τP(r) is a prefix of r.
  2. (b) · If |r| ≤ P, then τP(r) = r.
  3. (c) · If |r| > P, τP(r) is valid UTF-8 and is empty or has P − 3 to P bytes.
  4. (d) · If r is valid UTF-8, so is τP(r), and it is not empty: no letter is split, and a valid token is never cut to nothing.
  5. (e) · τP(τP(r)) = τP(r).
  6. (f) · If |r| > P and τP(r) is empty, then r is not valid UTF-8.

Proof. (a), (b), (c) and (e) can be read off the rule. For (d): a cut keeps valid text valid exactly when it falls between letters, that is, when the byte at the cut is not a continuation byte (80–bf). A letter is a lead byte plus at most three continuation bytes, so one of the cuts P, P − 1, P − 2, P − 3 falls between letters. (f) is (d) read backwards. ∎

For BrahmicTokenizer the longest token has 32 bytes, so at P = 32 and P = 64 the cut never changes anything ((b)). The properties matter for G3's tokenizer v0 or a smaller P. proof.md also proposes a rule τ′ that keeps the bytes of a broken long token instead of emptying it; whether KE2 should do that is a question for TSAI. Checked by tests/test_lemma2.py: both rules on 5,000 raw-byte strings and 5,000 valid UTF-8 strings per P, more than 500 of them really cut to nothing, and the 36-byte example.

Worked example · the cut rule at P = 32
  • Our tokens. A, B and C have 7, 4 and 4 bytes, so (b) keeps them whole. So does every BrahmicTokenizer token: the longest has exactly 32 bytes.
  • A long valid token. 30 × a then भारत is 42 bytes. Cutting at 32 or 31 would split भ, so the rule keeps 30 bytes ((c), (d)).
  • A long broken token. The 36 bytes 95 + 20 × a + ಕನ್ನಡ start with 95, a continuation byte with nothing before it. Every start of 29 to 32 bytes is therefore broken, so the rule keeps nothing ((f)). Try it in the playground below.

Lemma 1, step 1 · the lit cells

Every byte gets its own cell, and the cells spell the string

In plain words

For a string of L bytes, the grid has exactly L lit cells, one in each position 0 to L − 1, all holding the same value 1/√L. From the lit cells you can read every byte back. So two different strings always light different cells.

The idea

Think of a seating chart with one column of seats per position. Each byte sits in its own column, in the row of its value. Two people could share a seat only if they were in the same column, and every column holds just one person. So no seat is ever shared, and the chart tells you exactly who sat where.

The statement · in proof.md, Lemma 1, steps 1 and 4; part 4 is an addition from proof_explained.md

For a cut string s of length 1 ≤ L ≤ P:

  1. x has exactly L nonzero entries, each equal to 1/√L, at the cells sp·P + p for 0 ≤ p < L.
  2. Position p (the cells v·P + p) holds exactly one lit cell if p < L, and none if p ≥ L.
  3. s can be read back: L is the number of lit cells, and sp = ⌊c / P⌋ for the lit cell c with c mod P = p.
  4. Before normalizing, ⟨x(a), x(b)⟩ = (positions where a and b have the same byte) / √(|a|·|b|). In particular the sum of squares is 1.

So different strings light different cells. The empty string gives the zero vector, the only code with no lit cell.

Proof, step by step
  1. Every cell number c < 256P is c = q·P + r for exactly one 0 ≤ r < P, 0 ≤ q ≤ 255.Division with remainder: cells match (byte, position) pairs one to one.
  2. The cell of position p has remainder p, so different positions give different cells.The remainder of a cell is its position. Lit cells never meet, even when a byte repeats.
  3. x = (1/√L) × (L unit vectors at different cells).Nothing adds twice, nothing cancels: (1). Grouping the cells by remainder: (2).
  4. For a lit cell c: position = c mod P, byte = ⌊c/P⌋.Undo step 1 on each lit cell: (3), and so injectivity.
  5. The overlap of two unit cells is 1 when byte and position agree, and 0 otherwise.Summing over the positions gives (4). ∎

Byte e0 appears at positions 1 and 4: cells 7,169 and 7,172, same row, different columns. The same holds for a4. Seven lit cells, each 1/√7 = 0.37796.

Tokens B and C (4 bytes each): B lights cells 5,888, 7,169, 5,602 and 4,515; C lights 5,568, 7,169, 5,602 and 4,515. Only position 0 differs (byte b8 = 184 against ae = 174). They share 3 of 4 cells, so by part 4 their overlap is 3/√(4 · 4) = 0.75: close, but not equal.

Why strings must fit in P. Step 2 needs L ≤ P. A byte v at position P would land on cell v·P + P = (v + 1)·P + 0, the cell of byte v + 1 at position 0. The codec takes exactly P positions (codec.py:70), and Lemma 2 (b), (c) make every cut string fit. Without the position, ab and ba would collide.

Lemma 1, steps 2 to 5 · normalizing and reading back

Two values far apart: high on the lit cells, slightly negative everywhere else

In plain words

Normalizing turns every lit cell into the same high number and every other cell into the same slightly negative number. For every string length the high number is above 15.9 and the low one is between −0.063 and 0, so any cut-off in between finds the lit cells. proof.md uses the midpoint. A fixed cut-off of 8 works for every string, and still works if every number is off by almost 8.

The idea

Normalizing applies one shift and one stretch to all numbers. Almost all cells are empty, so the average is tiny. Empty cells (0) end up a little below it, so slightly negative. Lit cells (1/√L) end up far above it. Equal numbers stay equal, so there are only two values. Because the stretch divides by a spread of about 1/√D, the high value is about √(D/L) ≥ √256 = 16.

The statement · in proof.md, Lemma 1, steps 2 to 5 and the remark on floating point; parts 5, 6 and the fp16 half of 7 are additions from proof_explained.md

For a cut string with L = |s| ≥ 1, D = 256P, m = √L/D, v = (1 − L/D)/(D − 1), σ = √v + ε:

  1. Mean and spread depend only on L: m and σ above.
  2. Two values. The code is h = (1/√L − m)/σ on the lit cells and u = −m/σ elsewhere. The empty string gives 0.
  3. Signs. h > 0 > u, and h − u = 1/(√L σ).
  4. Gap. h − u ≥ √((D − 1)/P)/(1 + ε√(D − 1)) > 15.99 for P ∈ {32, 64}.
  5. Bounds for every length. For 1 ≤ L ≤ P: h > 15.93 and −0.0627 < u < 0.
  6. Reading back and its room for error. The cells above any cut-off θ between u and h are exactly the lit cells. If every number is off by less than min(h − θ, θ − u), that still holds. Midpoint: room ≥ 8.0; fixed θ = 8: room ≥ 7.93 for every string; sign rule θ = 0: room |u| ≥ 0.0078, and 0 for the empty string.
  7. Floating point. Rounding to bf16 or fp16 is monotone and keeps two values with the same signs, and h stays above 15.87.

Proof, step by step
  1. Σ xi = L·(1/√L) = √L ⇒ m = √L/D.L lit cells of 1/√L, the rest 0 (step 1).
  2. Σ (xi − m)² = Σ xi² − 2m Σ xi + Dm² = 1 − L/D ⇒ v.The sum of squares is 1 (step 1, part 4); divide by D − 1. This is (1).
  3. t ↦ (t − m)/σ is one map for every cell; L = 0 gives 0/ε = 0.Equal inputs give equal outputs, so there are two values. This is (2).
  4. h > 0 ⇔ 1/√L > √L/D ⇔ D > L; u < 0 ⇔ m > 0.True, since L ≤ P < 256P. This is (3).
  5. Gap = (1/√L)/σ with L ≤ P and σ ≤ (1 + ε√D)/√(D − 1).(1/√L)(1 − L/D) and √v both decrease in L; the extreme case L = P gives (4) and (5).
  6. |yi − ei| < δ ⇒ lit cells > h − δ ≥ θ, others < u + δ ≤ θ.So the cells above θ are the lit cells, and step 1 reads the string back. The empty string needs θ ≥ 0. With θ = 8: h − 8 ≥ 7.93 and 8 − u > 8. This is (6).
  7. Rounding to nearest is monotone, with relative error ≤ 2−8 (bf16) or 2−11 (fp16).Every h (15.93 to 128) and |u| (0.0078 to 0.0627) is a normal number in both formats, so h ≥ 15.935(1 − 2−8) > 15.87 and u stays negative. This is (7). ∎

Theorem 1 · the codec never causes a collision

Same code exactly when same cut string, and a shared code has one of five causes

In plain words

Two tokens get the same code exactly when they are fed the same cut string. So every shared code comes from the table, and there are only five ways for that to happen: both tokens are empty, a broken long token was cut to nothing, the raw bytes really are the same, broken bytes were printed as �, or two long tokens agree up to the cut.

The idea

The codec is a lossless packing: Lemma 1 reads any code back. If two different strings packed to the same code, reading that one code back would give two different strings, which is impossible. To find why two tokens share a string, ask a few questions in a fixed order and stop at the first yes.

The statement · proof.md, section 3

Let r, r′ be the raw bytes of two tokens, f, f′ the bytes a table feeds to the codec, and s = τP(f), s′ = τP(f′).

  1. Theorem 1. code(s) = code(s′) ⇔ s = s′. The codec adds no collisions of its own.
  2. Reading back. The lit cells give s back from its code, in fp32 and after a bf16 cast (proof.md); fp16 and a fixed cut-off of 8 work too (proof_explained.md).
  3. Corollary, the causes. If two different tokens share a code, the first of these that applies is the cause (pair_cause in src/proofs/forward.py):
  4. Real tokenizer (proof.md, section 4). Raw table: 131,072 distinct codes at P = 32 and 64, in fp32 and bf16. Decode table: 129,931, with 1,141 tokens in 10 groups, every pair bad_bytes_in.
CauseConditionWhat it meansIn collisions.csv
emptyboth fed strings are emptytwo empty tokens; both get the zero codeempty
cut_to_emptythe cut string is empty, a fed string is nota long token that is not valid UTF-8 was cut to nothing (Lemma 2 (f))none (the raw table cuts plain bytes)
same_rawr = r′the vocabulary holds the same bytes twiceduplicate_vocab, special_literal
bad_bytes_inr ≠ r′ but f = f′decode table only: broken raw bytes printed with U+FFFDdecode_collapse
truncationf ≠ f′ but τP(f) = τP(f′)one is longer than P, and they agree up to the cuttruncation
Proof, step by step
  1. (⇐) Equal strings give equal codes.The code is a function of the string.
  2. (⇒) Both cut strings have at most P bytes, so Lemma 1 applies.Lemma 2 (b) and (c). One code reads back to one string, so the strings are equal.
  3. Shared cut string empty: both fed strings empty → empty; otherwise → cut_to_empty.A non-empty fed string cut to nothing is longer than P by (b), and not valid UTF-8 by (f).
  4. Not empty, and r = r′ → same_raw.The vocabulary holds the same bytes twice.
  5. r ≠ r′ but f = f′ → bad_bytes_in.In the raw table f = r, so this happens only in the decode table, whose bytes are the raw bytes with broken parts replaced by U+FFFD (proof.md, section 4).
  6. Otherwise f ≠ f′ with equal cuts → truncation.By (b) one of them is longer than P, and by (a) the cut string is a start of both. Each question splits what is left, so exactly one cause applies. ∎

Task 4 · Determinism

Decode everything three times and compare fingerprints

The lab askedDecode every token ID on CPU three times. Write the three hashes in teams/04-ke2/results/decode_cpu_sha256.txt. They must match.

In plain words

A hash is a fingerprint of data: 64 characters that change completely if even one byte changes. The team decodes all 131,072 tokens in three separate runs, fingerprints each result, and compares the three fingerprints.

Why it matters

Later weeks and other teams build on these tables. If decoding gave different answers on different runs or machines, nothing built on top could be trusted.

How the team did it

  1. Start three fresh Python processes, one after another, so nothing carries over between runs (src/determinism/tokenizer_decode_cpu.py, Avnish, #54).
  2. Each run checks the tokenizer file's SHA-256, then decodes every id in ascending order with decode([id]), special tokens included.
  3. It fingerprints the result with SHA-256: the line ke2-decode-cpu-v1, then for each id its number and its byte length, 4 bytes each, largest byte first, then the bytes.
  4. The parent compares the three hashes, and writes them only if they agree.
  5. An optional second check runs the forward codec three times on an Apple GPU (MPS) and compares it with the CPU (src/determinism/codec_v1_cpu_mps.py).
Worked example · what our tokens put into the fingerprint

Each run joins the whole decode table into one long byte string: the line ke2-decode-cpu-v1, then, token by token in id order, the id and the length in 4 bytes each, then the bytes.

TokenIts decode bytesWhat goes into the string
A · 242020 e0 a4 8f e0 a4 9500 00 09 74 00 00 00 07 20 e0 a4 8f e0 a4 95
B · 39329ef bf bd e0 af 8d00 00 99 a1 00 00 00 06 ef bf bd e0 af 8d
C · 74642ef bf bd e0 af 8d00 01 23 92 00 00 00 06 ef bf bd e0 af 8d

00 00 09 74 is the number 2,420, largest byte first. The id and the length mark where each token starts and ends: without them, "ab" then "c" and "a" then "bc" would join into the same "abc". After all 131,072 tokens, SHA-256 turns the string into 64 hex digits. If one run printed even one of B's bytes differently, its fingerprint would change completely. All three runs gave 3bbeb193…8e57.

Result

All three decode fingerprints are identical: 3bbeb193…8e57. On the GPU, the forward codec gives the same hash in all three runs at P = 32 and 64, and agrees with the CPU to within 7.6 × 10−6 and 1.5 × 10−5.

The idea

Deterministic means the result depends only on the input, never on when or how the program runs. A fresh process rules out anything left over from an earlier run, and comparing one fingerprint of the whole vocabulary checks every byte at once.

The maths
  • Run r computes X(r) = (fdec(0), …, fdec(V − 1)) in a fresh process.
  • S(X) = "ke2-decode-cpu-v1⏎" ‖ id4(0) ‖ len4(x0) ‖ x0 ‖ id4(1) ‖ len4(x1) ‖ x1 ‖ …, with 4 big-endian bytes each. Reading the lengths splits S(X) back uniquely, so S(X) = S(Y) ⇒ X = Y.
  • hr = SHA-256(S(X(r))). Claim: X(1) = X(2) = X(3). Evidence: h1 = h2 = h3. A false match would need a SHA-256 collision.
  • The bytes on this page give the same hash; the page's builder refuses to build otherwise.

Gate 1

Putting it together: Gate 1 holds

The gateThe forward encode proof is checked, and each token has a unique code or a known collision cause.

Gate 1 is not one more task. It is what the four tasks prove together. On Saturday 31 Oct the lab checks it three ways: pytest teams/04-ke2/tests -q gives 0 failures, the forward encode proof is checked, and each token has a unique code or a known collision cause.

How the tasks add up to the gate

So

The maths
Gate 1  ≡  (all proof checks pass)  ∧  ∀t:  [ ∀s ≠ t : EP(s) ≠ EP(t) ]  ∨  [ cause(group of t) is known and its check passes ]

Raw table: Theorem 1 plus 131,072 different rows give the first bracket for every t, at P = 32 and 64. Decode table: the 1,151 tokens in groups meet the second bracket (10 of 10 groups are decode_collapse, 0 other); the other 129,921 meet the first.

Tests

The team's test suite, and five checks in your browser

The lab askedPut the tests in teams/04-ke2/tests/. pytest teams/04-ke2/tests -q gives 0 failures.

In plain words

The team's tests check every result: the tables, the collision audit, the proof on synthetic strings and on the real tokenizer, the reference decoder, and the determinism scripts. One command runs them.

How they are built

Tests that need the real tokenizer find it through KE2_TOKENIZER (a folder with tokenizer.json and special_tokens_map.json) and skip without it; nothing is downloaded on its own. The optional GPU check runs only when asked.

What they cover

  • The tables: shapes, the known issue and the fix, no truncation, P = 64 equal to P = 32 padded, and agreement with upstream (test_tables.py).
  • The collision audit: every group is real, the causes, zero other, the committed CSV is current (test_collisions.py).
  • The proof: Lemma 1, Lemma 2 and Theorem 1 on synthetic strings, and on the real tokenizer (test_lemma1.py, test_lemma2.py, test_theorem1.py, test_proof_checks.py).
  • The reference decoder, determinism, the GPU codec check and the experiment runner.

For other teams

What G5 and G6 receive

The lab askedGive the KE2 output shape to G5 by Tue 27 Oct (output_shape.md). Give a decode reference to G6 by Wed 28 Oct (src/decode_ref.py).

G5: the output shape

G5 builds the model around KE2, so they need its input and output shapes, the trainable size, and the memory it uses. output_shape.md gives these for P = 32 and 64, with P = 32 recommended. The calculator below follows the same formulas.

G6: the decode reference

G6 is the performance team. They get a slow but obviously correct reference: src/decode_ref.py scores a code against every token's code by cosine, in float64, and returns the best token with its margin over the second best (Dattatreya, #99). Any faster decoder can be checked against it. On the raw tables it recovers all 4,096 sampled ids at P = 32 and 64, with the smallest margin 0.0318 (experiment.md, decode_ref.md).

The maths behind both handoffs
  • Parameters: KE2 learns D·d = 256·P·d numbers; a lookup table learns V·d. The ratio is V/(256P): 16 at P = 32 and 8 at P = 64.
  • Two-value shortcut (from Lemma 1, step 3; decode_ref.py scores with the same structure): E W⊤ = Σi Ei W:,i = hL Σi∈S W:,i + ℓL Σi∉S W:,i = (hL − ℓL) Σi∈S W:,i + ℓL Σi W:,i.
  • Memory: the code for N tokens takes N·D·4 bytes in float32 (32 KiB per token at P = 32), and it is kept for the backward pass.
  • Decoding (G6): decode_ref.py ranks all 131,072 tokens by cosine. For a clean code, the proof's read-back (Lemma 1, step 5) followed by a lookup in the raw table is an exact alternative, because all raw rows differ. Playground 6b shows it.

Rationale

Decisions and why

DecisionWhereWhyAlternative considered
Read raw bytes from the vocab piece#7This gives exact bytes for every token, including pieces of characters, which fixes the known issue at its source.Patching decode([id]). A printout of half a character has already lost the bytes.
Use upstream's encoder unchanged, pinned by commit#99The proof then covers what the team will train with.Re-implementing the encoder, which would prove a copy correct.
Build both tables at both P#7This measures the known issue and shows that P = 64 buys nothing here.Raw table only. The size of the known issue would go unmeasured.
Commit the tables, compressed#99Anyone can load the exact tables. Compressed .npz keeps them under the 5 MB limit with identical content hashes.Rebuilding them on every machine.
Pin the tokenizer by SHA-256, and never download on its own#99Everyone decodes identical files, and tests skip rather than fetch.Loading "latest" from the hub. Results could change underneath us.
Name each collision's cause, and require zero other#7, #99"Known cause" becomes something a test checks.Labelling by pattern only, such as "the row contains ef bf bd".
Prove injectivity by reading the string back#75This handles normalizing directly, and gives an algorithm the tests run.A counting or linear-algebra argument, which stops before normalizing.
Check in fp32 and bf16, on synthetic strings and on the real tokenizer#75The real vocabulary produces only one cause; a synthetic vocabulary plants all five.Real data only, which leaves four of the five causes unchecked.
Propose a safer cut rule, but keep the repository's#75The repository rule can empty a broken long token. Whether KE2 should keep its bytes instead is a question for TSAI.Changing upstream behaviour unilaterally.
A reference decoder by exhaustive float64 cosine#99Slow but obviously correct and deterministic, with a margin G6 can compare against.A fast decoder, which would need its own reference.
Three fresh processes for determinism#54This rules out anything left over between runs.Three runs in one loop, which could agree only because they share state.
Recommend P = 32output_shape.mdThe longest token is 32 bytes, so every code is already unique. P = 64 doubles parameters and memory for no gain.P = 64 "for safety".
Explain with figures drawn from the codec#90proof_figures.py computes every number it draws and stops if the codec and the formulas disagree.Hand-drawn figures, which can drift from the code.
Add bounds for every length and the room for error#90They hold for any tokenizer that fits in P, and give the margins week 2's noisy decoding will need.Checking only the lengths that occur.
Scope

Limits and open inputs

  • Proven: Lemma 1, Lemma 2 and Theorem 1 for strings of at most P bytes (proof.md); the bounds for every length and the room for error (proof_explained.md).
  • Checked, not proven: that the printout equals the raw bytes with broken parts replaced, for all 131,072 ids (proof.md, section 4); bf16 in the tests; fp16 and the noise example in src/docs/proof_figures.py.
  • Cut rules differ: the decode table steps back over continuation bytes, the raw table cuts plain bytes, and the proof uses the repository rule. None cuts anything for this tokenizer; revisit when it changes (README.md).
  • G3's tokenizer v0: set KE2_TOKENIZER and re-run src/run_experiment.py. The proof does not change; the counts may.
  • G10's special-token list: the 356 special tokens are encoded from their literal text. The final policy can change what is fed to the codec, not the theorem.
  • Not in Week 1: decoding a code predicted by a model (week 2), training, and the KE2 decision on 14 Nov.

Background

Concepts from scratch

Eight ideas carry the whole of Week 1, and the task sections link here when they use one. Each is explained four ways: in plain words for anyone, the idea for why it works, an example, usually our token A, B or C, and the maths for the exact statement the code and the proofs rely on. Each builds on the one before.

1. Tokens

In plain words

A language model does not read letters. It reads text as a list of numbered pieces called tokens. BrahmicTokenizer-131K has 131,072 different tokens: whole words such as भारत, parts of words, punctuation, emoji, and some pieces smaller than one character.

The idea

The token list works like a dictionary of word parts. Common words get their own entry. Rare words are spelled with several smaller entries, and very rare characters are spelled byte by byte. That way a finite dictionary can write any text at all.

Example

A comes from भारत एक देश है ↦ (66526, 2420, 13092, 732): four whole words. B comes from மிஸ் ↦ (4475, 19844, 39329): a rarer word spelled with three pieces, and the last piece starts in the middle of a letter.

The maths

The tokenizer is a function from text to a list of ids: text ↦ (t1, …, tn), with every ti ∈ {0, 1, …, V − 1} and V = 131,072. Each id t stands for a byte string f(t). The tokenizer loses nothing: f(t1) f(t2) … f(tn) = UTF-8(text), the text's bytes joined in order.

2. Bytes and UTF-8

In plain words

A computer stores every character as one to four small numbers between 0 and 255, called bytes. Bytes are usually written in hexadecimal (base 16), two digits each: e0 means 14 × 16 + 0 = 224.

The idea

UTF-8 marks the job of each byte in its first bits. A reader can always tell where a character starts and how many bytes it needs. So a piece that stops early is visibly incomplete, and that is exactly what later prints as �.

Example

ஸ is U+0BB8 = 0000 1011 1011 1000. In the 3-byte pattern: 11100000 10101110 10111000 = e0 ae b8. Token 19844 ends with e0 ae and token B starts with b8. On its own, B begins with a continuation byte: broken.

The maths
Code pointsBytesBit patternExamples
U+0000 – U+007F10xxxxxxxa = 61
U+0080 – U+07FF2110xxxxx 10xxxxxxé = c3 a9
U+0800 – U+FFFF31110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxxभ = e0 a4 ad
U+10000 – U+10FFFF411110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx😀 = f0 9f 98 80

Worked example: भ is code point U+092D = 0000 1001 0010 1101 in binary. Fill its 16 bits into the 3-byte pattern: 11100000 10100100 10101101 = e0 a4 ad.

A byte string is broken (not valid UTF-8) if a start byte lacks its continuation bytes (e0 a4), a continuation byte 80–bf stands alone, or it uses a byte UTF-8 never uses (c0, c1, f5–ff).

3. Pieces and the byte map

In plain words

Inside the tokenizer file, each token is written as a piece: one visible stand-in character per byte. Token 2420, " एक", is written Ġà¤ıà¤ķ.

The idea

Some bytes are invisible, like the space, or are not characters on their own, like e0. Swapping each of the 256 bytes for its own printable character lets every token be written as text, and the swap can be undone exactly. Undoing it gives the token's true bytes, which is how the raw byte table is built.

Example

B's piece is ¸à¯į. The byte map reads it back as b8 e0 af 8d: ¸, à and ¯ are printable and stand for themselves; į stands in for 8d, one of the 68 swapped bytes.

The maths

The byte map β : {0, …, 255} → 256 printable characters is a bijection (one-to-one and onto). The 188 bytes that are already printable (33–126, 161–172, 174–255) map to themselves. The other 68 map to U+0100, U+0101, … in order; for example 20 ↦ Ġ. The raw bytes of a token are fraw(t) = β−1(piece(t)), applied character by character.

Example: Ġ à ¤ ı à ¤ ķ ↦ 20 e0 a4 8f e0 a4 95.

4. Embeddings, and what KE2 changes

In plain words

A model needs a list of numbers for every token. Normally it learns and stores a separate list for each of the 131,072 tokens. KE2 instead computes a fixed code from the token's bytes, then learns one shared layer that turns codes into the model's numbers.

The idea

A lookup table must memorise every token separately. KE2 learns how byte patterns map to meaning, so tokens that share spelling share structure. The number of learned values no longer grows with the size of the vocabulary.

Example

With a model width of d = 1,024, a lookup table learns 131,072 × 1,024 ≈ 134 million numbers. KE2 at P = 32 learns 8,192 × 1,024 ≈ 8.4 million, the same for every token, including A, B and C.

The maths

Lookup table: x = Wemb[t] with Wemb ∈ ℝV×d, so V·d learned numbers. KE2: x = W · EP(t) with W ∈ ℝd×D, D = 256 · P, and EP fixed, so D·d learned numbers. At P = 32, V/D = 131,072 / 8,192 = 16, so KE2 learns 16 times fewer numbers (8 times at P = 64).

5. The grid code

In plain words

Picture squared paper with 256 rows, one for each possible byte value, and P columns, one for each position. For a token, shade one square in each column: the row of the byte at that position. Then all the shaded squares get the same value.

The idea

The row says which byte; the column says where it is. Keeping the column is what keeps order: ab and ba shade different squares. Each column gets exactly one shade, so shades never pile up.

Example

A at P = 32 shades 7 squares, one per column: (byte 32, column 0), (224, 1), (164, 2), (143, 3), (224, 4), (164, 5), (149, 6). Those are entries 1,024, 7,169, 5,250, 4,579, 7,172, 5,253 and 4,774, each 1/√7 = 0.378.

The maths

Let cv ∈ ℝ256 be 1 at entry v and 0 elsewhere, and ep ∈ ℝP be 1 at entry p. Their Kronecker product cv ⊗ ep ∈ ℝ256P is 1 at exactly one entry, number v·P + p. This product gives the method its name. For a row b = (b0, …, bL−1):

κP(b) = 1√L Σp < L cbp ⊗ ep

Example: hi at P = 32 marks entries 104·32 + 0 = 3328 and 105·32 + 1 = 3361. In the repository: codec.py line 85, lin_idx = bytes_long * pos_dim + pos.

6. Normalizing

In plain words

After shading, all 256 × P numbers are shifted and stretched so that their average is 0 and their spread is 1.

The idea

It is the same shift and the same stretch for every number, like converting a list of temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit at once. Numbers that were equal stay equal, and the bigger one stays bigger. So shaded squares can still be told apart from empty ones.

Example

A's 8,192 numbers are 7 of 0.378 and 8,185 zeros. The mean is 0.000323 and the spread 0.011045. After the shift and stretch, the 7 marks are 34.19 and every other entry is −0.0292.

The maths
μ(x) = 1D Σi xi,   σ(x) = √( Σi (xi − μ)² ⁄ (D − 1) ),   z(x) = x − μσ + ε,   ε = 10−6

The forward encode is EP = z ∘ κP: build the marks, then normalize (codec.py lines 101–104). σ divides by D − 1, PyTorch's default.

7. One-to-one, collisions and decoders

In plain words

A rule is one-to-one if different inputs always give different outputs. A collision is two inputs with the same output. Week 1 asks whether the code is one-to-one on tokens, and if not, why not.

The idea

The cleanest way to prove there are no collisions is to show the rule can be undone. If a decoder always recovers the input from the output, two different inputs cannot share an output. The decoder would have to return two answers for one code.

Example

Printing is not one-to-one: B and C both print as �். Reading raw bytes is one-to-one on this vocabulary: all 131,072 rows differ. The decoder recovers A's bytes from A's code, so no other row can have A's code.

The maths

f is injective (one-to-one) if f(a) = f(b) ⇒ a = b. If some g satisfies g(f(a)) = a for every a (a left inverse; here, the decoder), then f is injective:

f(a) = f(b)  ⇒  a = g(f(a)) = g(f(b)) = b.

This is the whole strategy of Theorem 1. For V tokens, codes lost = V − (number of different codes).

8. Fingerprints

In plain words

A fingerprint (hash) turns any amount of data into 64 characters. Change one byte of the data and the fingerprint changes completely.

The idea

To check that two huge results are identical, compare their fingerprints. Matching fingerprints mean matching data, because finding two different inputs with the same fingerprint is practically impossible.

Example

SHA-256 of abc is ba7816bf…f20015ad; of abd it is a52d159f…298449c9. One letter changed, every digit changed. Task 4 compares three such fingerprints of the whole decode table.

The maths

SHA-256 is a function H from byte strings to 256-bit values (64 hex digits). No two inputs with the same output have ever been found; a generic search needs about 2128 tries. To fingerprint a list of tokens, first join it with a length in front of each item, S(X) = len4(x0) ‖ x0 ‖ len4(x1) ‖ x1 ‖ …. This can be split back in only one way, so H(S(X)) = H(S(Y)) means X = Y.

Reference

Glossary

Every term this page uses, in plain words. Come back here whenever a word is unfamiliar.

Text and bytes

Tokenizer
The program that cuts text into tokens. Here it is BrahmicTokenizer-131K, built for Indian languages, English and code.
Token
One numbered piece of text: a word, part of a word, a symbol, or part of a character.
Token id
The number of a token, from 0 to 131,071.
Vocabulary
The full list of 131,072 tokens the tokenizer knows.
Special token
A token with a reserved job, such as <|begin_of_text|>. There are 356; they are stored as their literal text.
Byte
A small number from 0 to 255. Computers store all text as bytes, usually written in hex: e0 is 224.
UTF-8
The rule that turns each character into 1 to 4 bytes: a is 1 byte, भ is 3, 😀 is 4.
Piece
How the tokenizer file writes a token: one stand-in character per byte, so any byte can be written down.
Fragment
A token that holds only part of a character, for example the first 2 of its 3 bytes. Tokens B and C start with the last byte of a letter.
Start byte, continuation byte
In UTF-8 a character opens with a start byte that says how long it is, followed by continuation bytes 80–bf. A continuation byte with no start byte in front is broken.
Pulli (virama)
The Tamil sign ் that removes a letter's vowel. In tokens B and C it follows the stray byte.
Script class
The writing system a token belongs to (Devanagari, Tamil, Latin and so on), worked out from its bytes. "Fragment: Tamil" is a piece whose bytes point to Tamil.
� (U+FFFD)
The replacement mark a computer prints when bytes do not form a complete character.

Tables and codes

decode([id])
Asking the tokenizer to print one token as text. The repository builds its rows this way today.
Decode table
One row per token, made from its printout. It has the known issue.
Raw byte table
One row per token, made from the token's true bytes. It is the fix.
Row
The bytes the encoder reads for one token, at most P of them.
P
The number of byte positions (columns) in a code: 32, the repository's default, or 64. A code has 256 × P numbers.
Truncation, cut rule
Cutting a row longer than P bytes without splitting a character (τP, the repository's utf8_safe_truncate). Never needed here: the longest token is 32 bytes.
Embedding
The list of numbers a model uses to stand for a token. Usually learned and kept in a big table.
KE2
Kronecker Embedding 2: computing a token's numbers from its bytes with the kronecker-embeddings code, followed by one trainable layer.
Code, forward encode
The 256 × P numbers computed from a row: one mark per byte, then normalized. Computing it is the forward encode; the program doing it is the encoder.
Normalize
Shift and scale a list of numbers so its average is 0 and its spread is 1. After this a code has just two values.
Mark, support
A mark is the one grid entry a byte switches on. The support is the set of a row's marks; Lemma 1 shows it spells out the row.
Kronecker product
A way of combining two lists into one long list. Here it combines "which byte" with "which position" into one grid entry.
Cut-off (threshold), sign rule
Reading back keeps the cells above a cut-off. proof.md uses the midpoint of the two values; a fixed 8 works for every string; 0, the sign rule, works on clean codes but not on noisy ones.
Decoder
The reverse of the encoder: it reads the bytes back from a code. src/decode_ref.py is the team's reference for G6; it ranks every token by cosine.
Collision
Two or more tokens with the same code.
Collision group, codes lost
A set of tokens that share one code. Codes lost = number of tokens minus number of different codes.
Cause
Why tokens share a code. proof.md names five: empty, cut_to_empty, same_raw, bad_bytes_in and truncation. collisions.csv calls bad_bytes_in decode_collapse.

Checking

Proof, lemma, theorem
A proof is an argument that a statement is always true. A lemma is a smaller step used to prove the main result, the theorem.
Numerical check
Running the real code on real data to confirm what a proof says.
Unique, one-to-one
No two different inputs give the same output. The proof shows the encoder is one-to-one on rows.
float32, bf16, fp16
Ways to store each number: float32 keeps about 7 digits; bf16 and fp16, used for training, keep 2 to 3. The codes still read back exactly after rounding to them.
Hash, fingerprint
A 64-character summary of data (SHA-256). Change one byte and it changes completely.
Deterministic
Gives the same answer every time it runs.
CPU, process, thread
The computer's main processor; one running copy of a program; one of several workers inside it. Task 4 varies the last two.
Test, pytest
A test is a small program that runs the code and checks the answer. pytest runs them all with one command.

The lab

Gate 1
The Week 1 milestone: the forward encode proof is checked, and each token has a unique code or a known collision cause.
Tokens A, B, C
This page's running example: A = 2420 (" एक"), B = 39329 and C = 74642 (two Tamil pieces that both print as �்).
Known issue
Tokens that hold part of a character all print as �, so the repository gives them one shared code. The raw byte table fixes it.
kronecker-embeddings
The starting repository. Its encoder, kronecker_codec, is used unchanged.
Repository, commit
A folder of code with its full history; a commit is one saved version, named by a code such as 7dfcf39.
G3, G5, G6, G10
Other lab teams, numbered like the folders in era-v5-lab/teams/: G3 tokenizer, G5 architecture, G6 performance, G10 post-training.
pr-guard
The lab's automatic check on pull requests: files in topic folders, none over 5 MB, no email addresses.
